purpose: Historical evidence from superseded artifacts; not current evaluation outputs.

text: Research note for Bashir Sadeghi  •  24 November 2026

Semantic distance adds useful information about wording and meaning, but it can still overlook a changed number or an important word. We should report it alongside WER and CER and inspect concrete errors before using it to choose a model.

This audit reuses the same 500 AMI-Cleaned clips [3] and their 1,500 saved predictions from Whisper Turbo, Whisper large-v3, and FUTO on CPU. No speech model was run again. The purpose is to understand what each metric tells us for part 3 of the take-home exercise.
The three scores answer different questions

WER counts word insertions, deletions, and substitutions. CER does the same at character level. Both are reported after leaderboard normalization. Semantic distance compares lightly cleaned original sentences using MiniLM embeddings: distance = 1 − cosine similarity. Lower is better for all three; semantic distance is not an error percentage or a probability of correctness. [1, 2]

FUTO has the lowest value on all three metrics in this sample. This audit does not establish statistical significance. WER and CER pool all word or character edits; semantic distance gives each clip equal weight, so the three columns have different scales and weighting.
How often do WER and semantic distance disagree
For each clip, we compared each pair of models. A reversal means WER prefers one prediction while semantic distance prefers the other. We excluded comparisons tied on either metric.

There are 98 reversals among 609 comparisons without ties (16.1%), involving 62 distinct clips. The other 891 of 1,500 pair comparisons are tied on at least one metric. These comparisons share clips and models; they are not independent trials. A reversal shows different preferences, not which metric is right.
Whisper large-v3: “Which is the highest, isn't it?”

WER prefers Turbo: it makes two word edits out of five reference words, compared with three for large-v3. Yet “nice” loses the reference’s central idea, “highest.” Large-v3 keeps that idea, consistent with the semantic score’s preference.

Large-v3 is still imperfect: it changes “exactly” into a confirmation question. Semantic closeness does not make the transcript exact. When we apply the same leaderboard normalization before embedding, the preference remains: 0.727 for Turbo versus 0.149 for large-v3.
Equal word error counts can hide different errors
Reference: “Like, you know, develop prototype GUI.”
FUTO CPU: “Like, you know, develop prototype.”
Whisper large-v3: “like, you know, develop prototype Google”

Both make one word error: FUTO deletes “GUI”; large-v3 substitutes “Google.” WER treats them equally. The semantic score distinguishes the two outputs, assigning the lower distance to the deletion. Neither preserves the technical term. For someone searching meeting notes for a discussion of a graphical user interface, that missing detail may matter more than the overall sentence similarity.

In the first example, large-v3 has higher WER but lower CER than Turbo. CER reveals how much character content survives. It still does not measure the importance of the changed content, and a low CER does not establish that a model will be easy to fine-tune.
Numbers reveal limits of sentence similarity
A small score can contain a large amount error
Reference: “Well I think if we are gonna use a touchscreen uh we're gonna go way above the twelve and a half Euros.”
Whisper large-v3: “Well, I think if we're going to use a touchscreen, we're going to go way above the €12,500.”

The reference amount is €12.50; the prediction says €12,500. Under the scorer, that is one word substitution among 20 normalized reference words. Most of the sentence is preserved, so WER is only 5%. CER and semantic distance also need interpretation: none of these values expresses the financial size of the mistake.

For comparison, Turbo preserves the amount, scores 0% WER, and has semantic distance 0.069. Thus the semantic score does penalize large-v3 here, but it is not a guarantee that the amount is usable. After normalizing the text before embedding, the wrong-amount distance is 0.028.
A changed age can receive the preferred score
Reference: “And we're going to target uh sixty to to eighty year old customers.”
Whisper Turbo: “and we're going to target the 60 to 80 year old customers.”
FUTO CPU: “And we're going to target the sixty two to eighty year old customers.”

The reference appears to say ages 60 to 80, with a repeated “to.” FUTO’s “sixty two to eighty” naturally reads as 62 to 80. WER and CER tie, while the original-text semantic metric prefers FUTO. This is a concrete reason to inspect numbers rather than accept the smallest distance.

That preference flips when both texts are normalized before embedding: Turbo scores 0.017 and FUTO 0.040. Therefore this example is sensitive to the text representation, including how numbers are written. It does not prove that the encoder is always insensitive to age changes. The interpretation remains conditional on the written reference; the audio was not reviewed.
Negation and extra content need direct inspection
A change from friendly to not friendly
Reference: “Oh that's good, no, that's nice and friendly.”
Whisper Turbo: “Oh, that's good. Yeah, that's nice and friendly.”
FUTO CPU: “Oh, that's good. No, that's not so friendly.”

FUTO changes “nice and friendly” to “not so friendly.” Its semantic distance is higher than Turbo’s, by 0.025. There is no calibrated threshold that turns 0.101 into an acceptable transcript. The reference and prediction share “good” and “friendly” despite a consequential local change.

This score is also preprocessing-sensitive: after leaderboard normalization before embedding, FUTO scores 0.086 versus Turbo’s 0.099, reversing the preference. In a simpler real example, “Don’t believe it.” → “We believe it.”, FUTO receives distance 0.470 and WER 50%. The encoder can react to negation, but these cases do not support treating it as a reliable negation detector.
Extra content can retain the general topic
Whisper Turbo: “Geez, it's gonna fall off, it doesn't let you put it on.”

The prediction adds “it doesn’t let you put it on,” which is absent from the reference. WER exceeds 100% because the nine word edits exceed the seven normalized reference words. Semantic distance is 0.244: related wording can still accompany added content.

Without listening to the clip, we cannot determine whether the extra clause was invented, omitted from the reference, or affected by clip boundaries. This audit identifies the mismatch; it does not establish its acoustic cause.

We also created four text-only checks. Each compares a meaning-preserving rewrite with a change to a critical fact. These are invented examples, not model predictions, and they are excluded from all AMI counts and averages.
Negation. Reference: “We should approve this proposal.”
We ought to approve this proposal.
We should not approve this proposal.
Meeting time. Reference: “The meeting starts at nine.”
Report recipient. Reference: “Send the report to Alice.”
Budget amount. Reference: “The budget is fifteen euros.”

In all four checks, semantic distance prefers the intended meaning-preserving version. WER prefers the critical change in the negation and recipient checks, ties in the time check, and prefers the correct amount. The number normalizer turns “fifteen euros” and “15 euros” into the same text for WER and CER.

These checks support the reason for adding a semantic metric. Four deliberately chosen examples do not validate it for arbitrary negation, names, or numbers. The real age-range example on page 3 is a useful counterexample to any blanket claim of reliability.

For a team choosing ASR for meeting notes, WER measures word accuracy, CER reveals smaller spelling differences, and semantic distance helps identify outputs that preserve the general point. These examples support using all three while directly checking important amounts, names, and negation.
For verbatim transcription, omitted words still matter when the broad meaning survives. We have not calibrated an acceptable semantic distance or evaluated downstream user decisions.

The audit verified identical clip IDs and original references for all three systems. The totals are 5,473 normalized words and 25,943 characters, including single spaces. Recomputed corpus WER and CER match the saved summary exactly; mean semantic distances differ by less than 10⁻⁹. All 1,500 predictions are included; FUTO has five empty predictions and the Whisper files have none.

The cached MiniLM encoder used CPU float32, two threads, batches of 32, masked mean pooling, and L2 normalization. [2] The longest input had 67 tokens; none reached the 256-token limit. Identical strings score 0; one empty side scores 1 by convention. Cosine distance ranges mathematically from 0 to 2. Semantic ties use tolerance 10⁻⁶; WER ties use equal word-edit counts.

WER and CER use level 0; WER allows compound matching, such as “touchscreen” versus “touch screen.” [4] Semantic inputs only remove explicit non-speech annotations and collapse whitespace. Its flat normalization plot is therefore expected. Our extra normalized-embedding checks are diagnostics, not replacements. We use MiniLM rather than the original SemDist paper’s RoBERTa encoder. [1]

Examples were selected after inspecting predictions and scores. They illustrate possible behavior, not error-category prevalence. No audio review, independent human semantic labels, or semantic confidence intervals were produced. The sample uses seed 17 and 48 meeting-by-duration groups. It does not establish behavior outside AMI.

Bashir supplied the model runs and chose the evaluation direction. Codex computed the audit, checked reproduction, selected cases, and drafted interpretations. A second AI reviewed the method and arithmetic. These checks are not independent human validation.

WER and CER pool edits over reference words and characters. Semantic distance is the mean of 1 minus cosine similarity across clips. Lower is better; the semantic value is not a percentage or a calibrated measure of correctness. No speech model was run.
Clips per model: 500. These are supplied-data scores, without population extrapolation, confidence intervals, or a significance claim.

Comparable pairs have defined WER and no ties on either metric. Reversals mean WER and semantic distance prefer different models on the same clip. Pairs share clips and models; they are not independent trials. All tie and exclusion counts are in the JSON file.
Examples are selected for review, not evidence that either metric is right. Show strict paired WER/semantic ranking reversals, largest semantic gap first, one example per clip.
Reference: Which is the highest, exactly.
M1 prediction:  Which is nice, exactly.
M2 prediction:  Which is the highest, isn't it?
WER prefers M1; semantic distance prefers M2.
Review: What information changed, and would that matter for the intended use? Check the audio before attributing a mismatch to the model or reference.

WER prefers M1; semantic distance prefers M3.
Review: What information changed, and would that matter for the intended use? Check the audio before attributing a mismatch to the model or reference.

M3 prediction: No was also bizartic.
WER prefers M3; semantic distance prefers M1.

WER prefers M1; semantic distance prefers M2.
Review: What information changed, and would that matter for the intended use? Check the audio before attributing a mismatch to the model or reference.
Reference: Um there are a f a few little things.
M2 prediction:  There were a few little things
M3 prediction: Um through f a few little things.
WER prefers M2; semantic distance prefers M3.
Review: What information changed, and would that matter for the intended use? Check the audio before attributing a mismatch to the model or reference.

The default normalizer and MiniLM encoder target English. Semantic inputs remove explicit non-speech annotations and collapse whitespace, independently of WER/CER normalization. CER includes single spaces. The encoder uses CPU float32, masked mean pooling and L2 normalization; inputs above 256 tokens fail without truncation. Identical strings score 0; one empty side scores 1 by convention.

Empty normalized references have undefined per-clip WER/CER (N/A). Their insertion counts still contribute to corpus totals; they are excluded from WER-based example selection. All transcripts contribute to the semantic mean. No audio or human meaning labels are evaluated. Numbers, names and negation can be wrong despite a small semantic distance.
